1.open: Who first introduced you to a good friend, a favorite book, or a place you love, and what did they say that made you give it a try?
questions: John begins with "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (v. 1). Why might the writer call Jesus "the Word" instead of using his name right away?

Verse 5 says, "The Light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it." Translations differ on whether the darkness has not overcome or not understood the light. What does each idea add for you?
Verse 11 says, "He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him." Why do you think so many people missed him then? What makes it easy to miss him now?
Verse 12 says those who received him were given "the right to become children of God," and verse 13 says this is not by human will but "born of God." What do you notice about who does the work here?
Verse 14 says "The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us." What does it mean to you that God came close in a real human life instead of staying distant?
John the Baptist says, "I am not the Christ" (v. 20) and points others to Jesus. Why might it be hard to be the one who points instead of the one in the spotlight?

Jesus asks the two followers, "What do you want?" (v. 38), then invites them to "Come and see" (v. 39). Philip says the same to Nathanael (v. 46). How would you honestly answer Jesus's question today, even if your answer is mixed or unsure?
Nathanael asks, "Can anything good come from Nazareth?" (v. 46). Where have you seen doubt or questions treated with welcome instead of pressure, and what made the difference?
1.life: This week, take Jesus's question in verse 38 seriously. Set aside ten quiet minutes, write down honestly what you are looking for right now, and tell God about it. Then invite one person to come and see something good, like a meal, a gathering, or a conversation.
1.prayer: Thank God that the Word became flesh and lived among us, full of "grace and truth" (v. 14). Ask for open eyes to recognize him, and for honesty about what each of us is really looking for.
1.tip: Verse 1 is read differently by different groups of Christians, and someone may ask about it. Say plainly that Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant churches read it as the Word being fully God, while some groups read it differently. Then bring the group back to what the whole chapter shows about Jesus, and avoid turning the evening into a debate.

2.open: Think of a party or gathering where something went wrong. What happened, and how did it turn out?
questions: When the wine ran out, Jesus' mother simply told him, "They have no more wine" (v. 3). What does it say about her that she brought a small, embarrassing problem to Jesus? What small problems do you hesitate to bring to God?
Mary told the servants, "Do whatever He tells you" (v. 5). Then the servants filled the jars to the brim (v. 7). What do you notice about the part ordinary people play in this story?
The jars held water for ritual washing, and Jesus filled them with far more fine wine than a party could use. What does that tell you about how Jesus gives? Where have you seen generosity like that?
John says this first sign "revealed His glory, and His disciples believed in Him" (v. 11). What does this sign show you about who Jesus is?
Jesus said, "How dare you turn My Father's house into a marketplace!" (v. 16). The same Jesus who made wine at a party made a whip in the temple. How do these two scenes fit together for you?

The leaders asked for a sign, and Jesus answered with "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again" (v. 19). The disciples only understood after the resurrection (v. 22). Has something in your faith made sense only looking back?

Verse 24 says Jesus "did not entrust Himself" to those who believed because of the signs, "for He knew them all." What do you make of that? What is the difference between being impressed by Jesus and trusting him?
If you are honest, where do you feel more like the crowd watching wonders, or the leaders demanding proof, than like someone who has fully trusted? What would help you right now?
2.life: This week, bring Jesus one small, ordinary need you would normally handle on your own, the way Mary brought him the empty wine jars. Then notice how he answers, and tell the group next time.
2.prayer: Thank Jesus for being present at ordinary celebrations and ordinary shortages. Ask him to give you a trust that goes deeper than being impressed, and to make your heart a place where he is welcome.
2.tip: The temple scene can lead to a debate about whether Jesus was angry and whether anger can be holy. Keep the group on what he was protecting, which was people's access to God. Also, a line about wine can make some people uneasy, so let people hold their own convictions about alcohol and keep the focus on Jesus' generosity. If the symbolism of the jars comes up, say plainly that Christians read it differently: some see old rituals giving way to something new, others see a simple act of kindness and abundance.

3.open: Tell about a time you got a fresh start, like a new school, a new job, a move or a new year. What did you hope would be different?
questions: Nicodemus was a respected leader, yet he came to Jesus "at night" (v. 2). Why might someone with a lot to lose approach Jesus quietly? When have you felt that way?

Jesus says, "no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again" (v. 3). Nicodemus takes it literally and asks, "How can this be?" (v. 9). What do you think Jesus means, and what part of it is hard to picture?

Jesus compares the Spirit to the wind: "You hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it is going" (v. 8). What does it mean that new life from God is real but not something we can control or manufacture?

Verses 3 to 5 are read in different ways. Some tie being "born of water and the Spirit" closely to baptism, and others see the water as a picture of inner cleansing by the Spirit. How can your group hold different views here and still listen to each other?

Jesus says the Son of Man "must be lifted up" so that "everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life" (vv. 14, 15). What do you notice about the picture of simply looking and trusting, instead of earning?

"For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son" (v. 16). Verse 17 adds that God did not send him "to condemn the world, but to save the world through Him." How does that fit or clash with the way you usually picture God?

Verses 19 to 21 talk about people who prefer the dark because they fear their deeds "will be exposed" (v. 20). What makes it hard to step into the light? If you are unsure about faith or about God, what holds you back or keeps your questions alive?
John the Baptist says, "He must increase; I must decrease" (v. 30), and he is glad about it. Where in your life, at work, at church or at home, is it hard to take a smaller place?
3.life: Nicodemus brought his questions to Jesus, even if it was at night. This week, set aside ten quiet minutes to bring Jesus one honest question or worry, and then read John 3:16 slowly to end the time.
3.prayer: Thank God for loving the world enough to send his Son. Ask for a fresh start where you need one, and for the humility to say, "He must increase."
3.tip: Verse 36 ends with the words "the wrath of God remains on him," and verses 18 and 36 may stir fear or strong reactions, especially for someone worried about a loved one. Do not rush to explain it away or to argue it. Point back to verses 16 and 17, where God's aim is to save, and let people say honestly what troubles them.

4.open: Who is someone you ended up having a surprisingly good conversation with, maybe a stranger on a trip or in a waiting room?
questions: The woman is surprised that Jesus would ask her for a drink, since "Jews do not associate with Samaritans" (v. 9). What dividing lines, like politics, background or church tradition, make people hesitate to talk with each other today?

Jesus says, "If you knew the gift of God and who is asking you for a drink, you would have asked Him" (v. 10). Notice that he begins by asking her for something. What does that tell you about how he treats people?
Jesus says the water he gives will become "a fount of water springing up to eternal life" (v. 14). What do people reach for today to satisfy their thirst, and where have you seen it run dry?

In verses 16 to 18 Jesus names her past, and she stays in the conversation. Christians read her differently, some as a sinner gently confronted and others as an outsider treated with dignity. What do you notice in how Jesus speaks to her either way?
Jesus says "true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth" (v. 23). What does it look like to worship honestly, not just in the right place or with the right routine?

The woman leaves her water jar and tells the town, "Come, see a man" (vv. 28, 29). She does not claim to have all the answers, she just invites people. What would an honest invitation look like for you? If you are unsure what you believe, what questions would you bring along?
The Samaritans say, "we have heard for ourselves" (v. 42). Why does it matter that faith moves from hearing about Jesus to meeting him yourself?
The official "took Jesus at His word and departed" (v. 50) before seeing any proof. Where are you being asked to trust without seeing the outcome, and what makes that hard?
4.life: Think of one person you tend to avoid or keep at a distance. This week, take one small step toward them: a greeting, a question, or a shared cup of coffee. Listen more than you talk.
4.prayer: Thank God that Jesus comes to us as we are and offers water that truly satisfies. Ask for honest thirst, for open eyes toward people we overlook, and for trust in his word where we cannot yet see.
4.tip: Verses 16 to 18 can slide into guessing about the woman's morals, which the text never spells out. Say plainly that Christians read her differently, then steer back to what is clear: Jesus knows her fully, treats her with respect, and she is changed.

5.open: Think of a time you waited a long time for something, like a appointment, a call or a piece of news. How did you pass the time?
questions: Jesus asks the man, "Do you want to get well?" (v. 6). Why might that be a harder question than it sounds after thirty-eight years?
The man answers with a reason why it has not happened: "I have no one to help me into the pool" (v. 7). When you bring your needs to God, do you tend to give reasons, hopes, or nothing at all? Why?
Jesus heals with a word, and the man stands up and walks (vv. 8, 9). What does it say about Jesus that he skips the pool and the usual way of doing things?

The leaders see a man healed after thirty-eight years and say, "It is unlawful for you to carry your mat" (v. 10). How can good rules end up crowding out the good they were meant to protect? Where have you seen that today?

Jesus says, "To this very day My Father is at His work, and I too am working" (v. 17). Why did his listeners take this as a claim to be equal with God (v. 18), and how do you react to a claim that big?

In verse 24 Jesus says, "whoever hears My word and believes Him who sent Me has eternal life and will not come under judgment." What does it mean to you that this life is described as something that begins now?

Jesus says the Scriptures "testify about Me, yet you refuse to come to Me to have life" (vv. 39, 40). How can someone study the Bible closely and still miss the point? What helps you keep coming to Jesus himself?

Jesus asks, "How can you believe if you accept glory from one another?" (v. 44). Whose approval pulls at you most, and how does that affect what you are willing to believe or say? If you are honestly unsure about Jesus, what questions would you want to put to him?
5.life: Jesus asked a man what he really wanted. This week, set aside five quiet minutes and answer that question honestly to God: what do you want from him right now? Say it plainly, even if it feels small or unsure.
5.prayer: Thank God that Jesus meets people where they are stuck. Ask for honesty about what we want from him, and for freedom from needing other people's approval.
5.tip: Verses 17 to 23 are where Christians read Jesus' claims differently: most see him sharing God's own nature, while some see a Son uniquely sent and empowered but not equal. Say that in one line, keep the group on what the crowd heard and how Jesus responds, and don't try to settle it tonight. Also watch verse 14: don't let it become a claim that sickness is punishment for sin, since the text does not clearly say that.

6.open: What is a meal you still remember years later, and why has it stuck with you?
questions: Andrew points out a boy with "five barley loaves and two small fish" and asks, "what difference will these make among so many?" (v. 9). When have you felt that what you had to give was too small to matter? What happened?

The crowd followed because they saw the signs, but Jesus says they are looking for him "because you ate the loaves and had your fill" (v. 26). What do people, including us, tend to want from Jesus first?

The crowd asks what work God wants from them. Jesus answers, "The work of God is this: to believe in the One He has sent" (v. 29). How does that sit with you? Does it feel like a relief, a challenge, or something else?
Jesus says, "I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger" (v. 35). What do you find yourself hungry for these days, and where do you usually go to be fed?

Jesus says, "No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him" (v. 44). Christians read this differently: some hear God choosing who will believe, others hear God reaching out to everyone, who remain free to say no. What do you notice in the verse that makes you lean one way or the other?

Many of Jesus' followers said, "This is a difficult teaching. Who can accept it?" (v. 60). Is there something about Jesus or the Christian faith that you find hard to accept? Say it as honestly as you can, even if you are unsure.

Many turned back, and Jesus asked the Twelve, "Do you want to leave too?" Peter answered, "Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life" (vv. 67-68). What keeps you hanging on when faith gets hard? Is it more like Peter's answer, or something different?
6.life: Each day this week, before you eat your first meal, stop for a moment and ask Jesus to feed you with himself, not just the food on your plate. At the end of the week, notice what, if anything, felt different.
6.prayer: Thank Jesus for being the bread that gives life. Ask him to meet each person in the group in their real hunger, and to give honest faith to anyone who is struggling or unsure.
6.tip: Verses 53 to 56, about eating his flesh and drinking his blood, will likely lead to a debate about Communion. Say plainly that Catholic and Orthodox Christians read these words as speaking directly of Communion, while many Protestants read them mainly as receiving Christ by faith. Then bring the group back to verse 35 and Peter's answer in verses 68 and 69, so the evening is not spent settling a question the church has debated for centuries.

7.open: When you were a kid, who was the person that knew you best, and what did they know about you that others didn't?
questions: Jesus' brothers pushed him to put on a show, but John says, "even His own brothers did not believe in Him" (v. 5). Why can it be hard to take seriously someone you have known for years?
Jesus tells them, "My time has not yet come" (v. 6). Where do you feel pressure to hurry, prove something or go public before you are ready?

The crowd was split in whispers. Some said, "He is a good man," while others said, "He deceives the people" (v. 12). Which voice in that crowd sounds most like you right now: curious, doubtful, afraid or convinced? Say it as honestly as you can.
Jesus says, "If anyone desires to do His will, he will know whether My teaching is from God" (v. 17). What do you think he means, and how does it change the way someone might begin to explore faith?

Jesus says, "Stop judging by outward appearances" (v. 24). Some people dismissed him because of where he came from. What outward details do we use to write people off, and when has someone done that to you?
On the last day of the feast Jesus called out, "If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink" (v. 37). What are you thirsty for these days, and where have you been trying to find it?

The officers came back and said, "Never has anyone spoken like this man!" (v. 46), and Nicodemus asked for a fair hearing (v. 51). What makes it hard to listen fairly when the people around you have already made up their minds?
7.life: Jesus invites anyone who is thirsty to come to him. This week, set aside five quiet minutes each day to tell him honestly what you are thirsty for, even if you are not sure he is listening. If a friend or family member has a different view of Jesus, practice listening to them without arguing.
7.prayer: Ask Jesus to meet the thirst each person is carrying tonight. Ask for the courage to listen fairly and speak kindly when people disagree about him.
7.tip: Verse 38 is hard to read because Christians differ on whether the living water flows from the believer or from Jesus himself. Say that plainly in a sentence, then bring the group back to verse 37, where the invitation is clear and open to everyone. Also leave room for people who feel like the doubting crowd, and do not rush them toward an answer.

8.open: When did you last see someone get called out in public, in person or online? What did you think as you watched?
questions: The scribes and Pharisees "made her stand before them" (v. 3), and only the woman was brought. What does that tell you about how people can use someone else's failure for their own purposes? Where do you see that today?

Jesus says, "Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her" (v. 7). Then the accusers "began to go away one by one, beginning with the older ones" (v. 9). Why might the oldest leave first, and what would it take for you to put down a stone?

Jesus tells her, "Then neither do I condemn you," and then, "Now go and sin no more" (v. 11). How do you hear those two sentences together? Where is it hardest for you to believe that condemnation has really been lifted?
Jesus says, "I am the light of the world" (v. 12). What does it look like when someone is walking in the dark, and when has light helped you see something true?
The crowd asks, "Who are You?" (v. 25). If you could ask Jesus one honest question about who he is, or admit one thing you are unsure about, what would it be?

Jesus says, "the truth will set you free" (v. 32), and his listeners reply that they have never been slaves. Where are we quick to say we are fine, when something is quietly holding us? What does Jesus mean by "everyone who sins is a slave to sin" (v. 34)?

Jesus says, "before Abraham was born, I am" (v. 58), and his hearers pick up stones. Most Christians hear a claim that he is eternal and divine, while some groups read it only as saying he existed before Abraham. Why do you think his words struck his hearers so hard?
8.life: Think of someone you have been quick to judge or talk about in a negative way. This week, pray for them by name each day, and look for one small way to treat them with the mercy Jesus showed the woman.
8.prayer: Thank Jesus that he is the light of the world and that he does not throw stones. Ask for honesty about where you need his mercy, and for a gentler heart toward people you find it easy to condemn.
8.tip: Verse 44, where Jesus calls the devil the father of his opponents, can be hard to hear and has been misused against Jewish people. Say gently that Jesus and his opponents were all Jewish, that this was a sharp argument with particular people, and that most churches firmly reject using it against any group today.

9.open: What is something you were completely sure about, only to find out you had it wrong?
questions: The disciples ask, "who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?" (v. 2). Why do people still look for someone to blame when bad things happen? When have you heard it, or said it?

Jesus answers that "this happened so that the works of God would be displayed in him" (v. 3). Christians read that differently: some think God intended the blindness, others think Jesus is only refusing to assign blame. How do you hear it, and what do you find hard about it?
Jesus says, "I am the light of the world" (v. 5). What does light do for people who are stuck in the dark, and where do you most want that light right now?
The man's neighbors can't agree on who he is, and he keeps saying, "I am the one" (v. 9). Why might a changed life be hard for the people around us to accept?

His parents say, "He is old enough. Ask him," because they were afraid (vv. 21-23). What would it cost someone you know to speak up about faith? When have you stayed quiet because of fear, and what was that like?

Pressed by the leaders, the man says, "I was blind, but now I see!" (v. 25). He doesn't have all the answers, only his own story. What is one thing you can say you know, even if you are unsure about a lot else?
After the man is thrown out, Jesus "found" him (v. 35). What does it mean to you that Jesus went looking for him? Where do you need to be found?
In verse 41 Jesus says, "since you claim you can see, your guilt remains." How is admitting we can't see different from insisting we already do? What makes the first so hard?
9.life: This week, pick one area where you feel sure you are right, such as a disagreement or a person you have judged. Ask God to show you what you might be missing, and listen to someone's side of it before you respond.
9.prayer: Thank Jesus for being the light of the world and for seeking out people who have been pushed away. Ask him to open your eyes where you are blind, and to give courage to say simply what you know.
9.tip: Verse 3 can sting if someone in the room has lived with illness, disability or loss, since it may sound like God planned their pain. Say up front that Christians read it in more than one way, and that nobody has to explain why suffering happens. Keep the focus on Jesus meeting the man and not blaming him.

10.open: Who is someone whose voice you would recognize instantly, even in a crowded room, and why?
questions: In the picture of verses 3 and 4, the shepherd "calls his own sheep by name and leads them out." What does it mean to you that Jesus knows people by name?
Jesus says, "I am the gate" (v. 9). In the story, a gate lets sheep go in and out safely. What do you think he is offering to those who come through him?

Verse 10 says, "The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I have come that they may have life, and have it in all its fullness." What is the difference between a full life and one that is just survived?

A hired hand runs when the wolf comes, but Jesus says, "The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep" (v. 11). What does this tell us about how Jesus sees us, and what he is willing to do for us?

Jesus says, "My sheep listen to My voice; I know them, and they follow Me" (v. 27). What voices compete for your attention, and how do you tell which ones to trust? If you find it hard to hear his voice at all, you can say so.
In verse 28 Jesus says, "No one can snatch them out of My hand." When have you felt that you might slip away from God, and how does this promise land with you today?

The crowd is divided. Some say, "He is demon-possessed and insane," while others ask, "Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?" (vv. 20, 21). Which of these reactions feels closer to your own, whether now or at some point in your life?
Jesus says, "I and the Father are one" (v. 30), and his listeners take it as a claim to be God. Why did it provoke such a strong reaction then, and what does it mean for how we trust him now?
10.life: Set aside ten quiet minutes this week, without your phone, to listen for God. Read verses 27 to 29 slowly, then tell Jesus honestly where you want to follow him more closely and where you feel unsure.
10.prayer: Thank Jesus for being the good shepherd who knows us by name and gave his life for us. Ask him to help each person in the group recognize his voice and rest in his care.
10.tip: Verse 30 can pull the group into a long debate about the nature of God. Keep it simple: note that Christians have long read it as Jesus claiming to share God's own nature, and that his listeners clearly understood it that way (v. 33). Then bring the conversation back to the shepherd and the sheep, and give quieter people room to say they struggle to hear or trust his voice.

11.open: Think of a time you waited a long time for someone to show up. What was going through your mind while you waited?
questions: The sisters tell Jesus, "the one You love is sick" (v. 3). Then Jesus stays where he is for two more days (v. 6). What do you make of the delay, and how do you think the sisters felt about it?
Martha says, "Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died" (v. 21). Mary says the very same words (v. 32). Have you ever felt that way toward God? What did you do with that feeling?

Martha believes in a resurrection "at the last day" (v. 24). Jesus answers, "I am the resurrection and the life" (v. 25). What changes when hope is about a person and not only a future event? Christians differ on how much Jesus meant this as a present gift and how much as a future hope.
Jesus asks Martha, "Do you believe this?" (v. 26). Where is she honest in her answer, and how would you answer that question today, including any doubts you carry?
Verse 35 is the shortest verse in this chapter: "Jesus wept." Why do you think he cried when he knew he was about to raise Lazarus? What does that tell us about how he treats our grief?

Jesus tells the crowd, "Take away the stone" (v. 39), and later, "Unwrap him and let him go" (v. 44). Lazarus is alive, but he still needs help from others to be free. Where do you see people needing help to be set free, and how can a group like ours offer it?
After seeing the miracle, "many of the Jews" believed, but others went to the Pharisees (vv. 45, 46). Why might the same event lead people in such different directions?

Caiaphas says it is better "that one man die for the people" (v. 50), and the writer says he spoke more truly than he knew (vv. 51, 52). What do you notice about how God can work even through people who do not intend it?
11.life: Think of one person you know who is grieving or waiting on something hard. This week, sit with them, send a note, or call, and do not try to fix anything. Just be present, the way Jesus was at the tomb.
11.prayer: Bring God the place where you feel he has been slow or absent, and say it honestly, as Martha and Mary did. Ask him to meet you there, and thank him that he is "the resurrection and the life" (v. 25).
11.tip: Grief and doubt will likely come up, especially around "if You had been here." Do not rush to explain why Jesus waited. Let people say the hard thing out loud, point out that Jesus did not scold either sister for saying it, and be ready for the question of why Lazarus was raised when others are not. It is fine to say we do not fully know.

12.open: What is the most extravagant thing you have ever given or received as a gift?
questions: Mary pours out "about a pint of expensive perfume" on Jesus' feet, and the house is "filled with the fragrance" (v. 3). What does her act tell you about how she saw Jesus? What would a gift like that look like today?

Judas asks why the perfume was not sold and the money "given to the poor" (v. 5), but John says he did not care about them (v. 6). Why can a good-sounding objection still come from the wrong heart? When have you caught yourself doing this?

The crowd shouts "Blessed is the King of Israel!" (v. 13), yet Jesus arrives on "a young donkey" (v. 14). What kind of king does this show, and how does he differ from the king people may have wanted?
Jesus says, "unless a kernel of wheat falls to the ground and dies, it remains only a seed" (v. 24). Where have you seen something have to end or be let go before something new could grow?
Jesus admits, "Now My soul is troubled" (v. 27). What do you make of Jesus being honest about his distress? How does that sit with the way you bring your own fears to God?
Verse 32 says, "I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw everyone to Myself." What does it mean to you that the cross is where he draws people in?

Many leaders believed but did not say so, because "they loved praise from men more than praise from God" (v. 43). Where do you find it hard to be open about your faith? If you are unsure what you believe, what holds you back from saying so here?
Jesus says, "I have not come to judge the world, but to save the world" (v. 47). How does that change the way you picture him? What part of that is hard to believe?
12.life: Do one quiet, costly act of love this week for Jesus or for someone he loves, without telling anyone. It could be your time, money or attention. Then notice what it cost you and what you felt.
12.prayer: Thank Jesus for coming as a humble king who gave his life. Ask for courage to follow him, to let go of what you are gripping too tightly, and to be honest about where you are.
12.tip: Verses 37 to 40 about blinded eyes and hardened hearts may spark a long debate or leave someone anxious. Say plainly that Christians read these verses differently: some think God caused the unbelief, others think he confirmed a refusal already made. Then bring the group back to verses 44 to 47, where Jesus came to save and not to condemn.

13.open: Think of a time someone did something small and humble for you that you still remember. What was it?
questions: Verse 3 says Jesus knew "the Father had delivered all things into His hands," and then verse 4 says "He got up from the supper." Why do you think John puts these two things side by side?
Foot washing was a job for the lowest servant. What is the equivalent job today that people avoid, and what would it look like for you to do it for someone?
Peter says, "Never shall You wash my feet!" (v. 8). Why is it sometimes harder to receive help or grace than to give it?
Jesus answers, "Unless I wash you, you have no part with Me" (v. 8). What do you think he means, and what does it say about who does the work of making us clean?

Jesus says, "I have set you an example so that you should do as I have done for you" (v. 15). Some churches practice foot washing literally, and most read it as a picture of humble service in daily life. How might your group live out the heart of it either way?
Jesus washed the feet of Judas, knowing what Judas would do (vv. 2, 11). What do you make of that, and how does it shape the way we think about people who hurt us?
Jesus says, "As I have loved you, so you also must love one another" (v. 34). Who in your life is hardest to love this way, and what is one honest thing that makes it hard?

Peter promises, "I will lay down my life for You," and Jesus says he will deny him three times (vv. 37, 38). Where have you seen your own good intentions fall short, and what does Jesus' response to Peter suggest about how he sees us then?
13.life: This week, do one quiet, unglamorous act of service for someone without telling anyone, and let one person help you with something you would normally do alone.
13.prayer: Thank Jesus for loving his own "to the very end" (v. 1). Ask him to make you someone who serves with a humble heart and receives help with grace.
13.tip: Peter's denial and Judas's betrayal can pull the group into debating whether Judas could have been forgiven. Gently bring it back to what the chapter shows: Jesus served both of them, and he loves his friends even when he knows they will fail him.

14.open: When you were a kid, what helped you feel okay when a parent or someone you trusted had to go away for a while?
questions: Jesus begins, "Do not let your hearts be troubled" (v. 1). He says it again in verse 27. What do you think was troubling his friends that night, and what tends to trouble you?
Jesus says, "In My Father's house are many rooms" and that he is going to "prepare a place for you" (v. 2). What does it mean to you that he is getting a place ready for you personally?

Thomas says, "we do not know where You are going, so how can we know the way?" (v. 5). Why might it be a good thing that Thomas just said it out loud? What question would you like to ask Jesus right now?

Jesus answers, "I am the way and the truth and the life" (v. 6). Christians read the rest of that verse differently: some think only those who knowingly trust Jesus come to God, and others think people who never knowingly believed may still come to God through Christ. How do you hear the first part of the verse as good news, whatever else you think about it?
Philip asks to see the Father, and Jesus says, "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father" (v. 9). What does Jesus' life tell you about what God is like?

Jesus promises, "I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you" (v. 18). When have you felt alone or on your own in your faith? What would it look like for that promise to be true in that place?

Jesus says the Spirit "will teach you all things and will remind you of everything I have told you" (v. 26). Where have you noticed a thought, a verse or a nudge come back to you at just the right time? If you haven't, what is that like to hear?
Jesus says, "Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you. I do not give to you as the world gives" (v. 27). How is the peace Jesus gives different from the calm we try to create for ourselves?
14.life: Pick one worry that keeps coming back this week. Each time it shows up, say verse 27 quietly to yourself, "Do not let your hearts be troubled; do not be afraid," and hand that worry to Jesus in a sentence of prayer.
14.prayer: Thank Jesus for promising not to leave us alone and for giving us his peace. Ask him to make that peace real for each person in the group, especially for anyone who is anxious or struggling to believe tonight.
14.tip: Verse 6 can turn into a debate quickly. Say in one line that Christians read it differently, then bring the group back to what Jesus is doing here: comforting frightened friends and showing them the Father. Keep the question about him, not about who is in or out.

15.open: What is something you have tried to grow or keep alive, like a plant, a garden or a sourdough starter? How did it go?
questions: Jesus says, "I am the true vine, and My Father is the keeper of the vineyard" (v. 1). What does it tell you about God that he is pictured as a gardener who tends the vine?
Verse 2 says the Father "prunes" fruitful branches "to make it even more fruitful." Have you ever gone through a season of cutting back that later turned out to help you grow? What was that like?
Jesus says, "Remain in Me, and I will remain in you" (v. 4). What does staying connected to Jesus look like in an ordinary week for you, and what tends to pull you loose?
Verse 5 says, "apart from Me you can do nothing." Does that feel comforting, discouraging or something else to you right now? Be as honest as you like.

Verses 2 and 6 describe branches that are cut off and burned, and Christians disagree about what that means. Some think these are believers who can fall away. Others think they are people who only seemed connected and never truly were. What questions or worries does this image raise for you?
Jesus says, "love one another as I have loved you" (v. 12). Who in your life is hardest to love this way, and what would a small step toward them look like?
In verse 15 Jesus says, "I have called you friends." How is being a friend of Jesus different from being a servant, and does it feel believable to you?
Jesus warns, "If the world hates you, understand that it hated Me first" (v. 18). Where have you felt pushback or awkwardness for your faith, and how did you handle it?
15.life: Pick one connection in your week that really feeds you, like prayer, a friend, or time in the Bible, and protect it. Pick one that only looks like it helps, and cut it back a little.
15.prayer: Thank Jesus that he calls us friends and not just servants. Ask him to keep you joined to him, and to help you love the people around you the way he has loved you.
15.tip: Verses 2 and 6 can frighten people who already worry about whether they are good enough. Say plainly that Christians read these verses differently, then point the group to the surrounding words of welcome: "You are already clean" (v. 3) and "Remain in My love" (v. 9). Do not try to settle the debate in one evening.

16.open: Think of a time you waited for good news after a hard stretch. What did the waiting feel like?
questions: Jesus says, "I have told you these things so that you will not fall away" (v. 1). Why might it help to be warned about hard times before they come?
In verse 2 Jesus says some people who harm his followers will think "he is offering a service to God." What does that tell us about how sincere belief can still go wrong?
Jesus says, "it is for your benefit that I am going away" (v. 7). That must have sounded strange to his friends. When has something you didn't want turned out to carry some good?
Jesus calls the Spirit "the Spirit of truth" who "will guide you into all truth" (v. 13). How have you seen God guide you, whether through Scripture, other people, or a quiet sense of direction?
Jesus says, "I still have much to tell you, but you cannot yet bear to hear it" (v. 12). What does it say about Jesus that he lets his friends learn at their own pace?
The disciples keep puzzling over "a little while" and say, "We do not understand what He is saying" (v. 18). Where do you feel confused about God right now? Say it as honestly as you like.
Jesus says, "you will weep and wail while the world rejoices. You will grieve, but your grief will turn to joy" (v. 20). What does the picture of childbirth in verse 21 add to that promise?
Jesus ends with, "In the world you will have tribulation. But take courage; I have overcome the world!" (v. 33). How do you hold honest trouble and real peace together?
16.life: Think of one person you know who is going through a hard season. This week, reach out with a call, a message or a meal, and simply let them know you are with them. Pay attention to what peace looks like for you in your own hard moments.
16.prayer: Thank Jesus that he told us the truth about trouble and also gave us peace in him. Ask for the Spirit's help for anyone in the group who is grieving, confused or afraid right now.
16.tip: Verse 2 can be misused to talk about enemies or other groups. Keep the group on what Jesus is doing for his friends: preparing them, not pointing fingers. When the Spirit's role in verses 8 to 11 comes up, say plainly that readers differ on the exact meaning, and keep the focus on the comfort of the passage. Also note that "you will see me" is read differently: some take it as the resurrection appearances, some as his presence through the Spirit, some as his return. You do not need to settle it tonight.

17.open: Who is someone who prayed for you or cheered you on at an important moment, and what did it mean to you?
questions: Jesus says, "this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent" (v. 3). How is that different from thinking of eternal life as simply living forever?
Jesus says, "I have revealed Your name to those You have given Me" (v. 6). What did the disciples see in Jesus that showed them what God is like? What has helped you understand what God is like?
Jesus prays for his friends knowing he is about to leave them, and he asks the Father to "protect them" (v. 11). What does it tell you about Jesus that his last prayer is so full of care for others?

In verse 15 Jesus says, "I am not asking that You take them out of the world, but that You keep them from the evil one." Where do you feel the pull between living in the world and staying true to your faith? What would it look like to stay present without losing your footing?
Jesus prays, "Sanctify them by the truth; Your word is truth" (v. 17). In plain words, what does it mean to be set apart for God? How might truth shape a person over time?

Jesus prays for those who "will believe in Me through their message" (v. 20). That includes us. How does it land to know Jesus prayed for you before you were born? If it is hard to feel that, what makes it hard?

Jesus asks "that all of them may be one, as You, Father, are in Me, and I am in You" (v. 21). Christians differ on whether this means one visible, organized church or a shared spiritual bond across many churches. What do you think unity could look like in your own church or neighborhood?

Jesus says unity is meant so "that the world may believe that You sent Me" (v. 21). When have you seen believers who were very different from each other treat one another well? What did that say to you?
17.life: Pick one believer you find hard to understand or agree with. This week, pray for them by name using Jesus' wish for unity, and look for one small, kind way to connect with them.
17.prayer: Thank Jesus that he prayed for his people on the night before his death, and that we are included. Ask God to protect your group, make you one, and help the people around you see his love through how you treat each other.
17.tip: Questions 7 and 8 can pull the group into a debate about denominations or which churches get it right. Name the disagreement in one line, then steer back to the practical question of how unity looks between people sitting in your own room.

18.open: Tell about a time you were in a room full of people you didn't know. What did you do to fit in or get through it?
questions: Jesus knew "all that was coming upon Him," yet he "stepped forward" to meet the soldiers (v. 4). What does that tell you about how he faced this moment? How do you tend to face things you know are coming?
Jesus tells the soldiers, "let these men go" (v. 8). Even while being arrested, he is looking out for his friends. What does that say about the kind of person he is?

Peter swings a sword in the garden, and Jesus answers, "Put your sword back in its sheath!" (v. 11). A few hours later Peter says "I am not" when asked if he is a disciple (v. 17). What do you think happened inside Peter between those two moments?
Peter is "warming himself" at a charcoal fire among the people who arrested Jesus (v. 18). Where are you most tempted to blend in and keep quiet about your faith: work, school, family, online?

When an officer slaps him, Jesus says, "If I said something wrong, testify as to what was wrong." (v. 23). What do you notice about how he responds to unfair treatment? What would it look like to answer mistreatment that calmly?

Jesus tells Pilate, "My kingdom is not of this world" (v. 36). Christians read this differently: some hear it as a rule that is mainly spiritual or still to come, others as a different kind of rule that refuses force but still shapes life now. What does the verse tell you about what kind of king Jesus is?

Pilate asks, "What is truth?" (v. 38). When has it been hard for you to tell what was true, and what helped you? If you are honestly unsure about Jesus, what is one question you would want to ask him?
18.life: Peter's failure happened while he was trying to stay warm and unnoticed. This week, watch for one moment when you are tempted to downplay your faith to fit in. Don't beat yourself up if you do. Tell God about it plainly and ask for his help next time.
18.prayer: Thank Jesus for choosing to drink the cup the Father gave him, and for staying faithful when his friends did not. Ask for honesty about your fears and for courage to follow him where it costs something.
18.tip: The chapter says "the Jews" several times, and it has been misused to blame Jewish people today. Remind the group that Jesus, Peter and every disciple were Jewish, and that John means particular leaders in Jerusalem, working with Rome. Say this briefly and calmly, then return to the questions.

19.open: Think of a time you went along with the crowd when you weren't sure you should. What was that like?
questions: Pilate says three times that he finds "no basis for a charge" against Jesus (v. 4), and still he gives way. What do you think pushes him to do it?
The soldiers mock Jesus with the words "Hail, King of the Jews!" (v. 3). In what way is the joke truer than they know?
Jesus tells Pilate, "You would have no authority over Me if it were not given to you from above" (v. 11). What does that tell us about how Jesus sees what is happening to him?
The chief priests say, "We have no king but Caesar" (v. 15). What are the modern versions of choosing safety or power over what we know is right?
Even in great pain, Jesus sees his mother and the disciple standing near and puts them in each other's care (vv. 26, 27). What does that moment show you about him?
Jesus says, "It is finished" (v. 30). Many readers take this to mean his work was complete, not only that his life was over. What do you hear in those words, and what questions do they raise for you?

Joseph and Nicodemus, who had been quiet or hidden followers, step forward after Jesus dies (vv. 38, 39). Why might it take something this heavy to move them? Where do you feel stuck between hiding and speaking up?

Christians have understood Jesus' death in different ways, and no single picture says it all. Which way of seeing the cross is most helpful to you right now, or do you honestly find it hard to make sense of?
19.life: Pick one quiet time this week, even five minutes, to sit with the cross. Read verses 28 to 30 slowly, then tell God honestly what you feel, whether it is thanks, sadness or confusion.
19.prayer: Thank Jesus for going to the cross for us. Ask for honesty about where we give in to pressure, and for courage like Joseph and Nicodemus to step forward.
19.tip: This chapter is heavy, and some will want to rush to Easter. Let the group stay with the sorrow for a while. When the question about how the cross saves comes up, say plainly that Christians understand it in different ways and let people share what helps them without settling it.

20.open: Think of a time you heard surprising news and could not quite believe it at first. What was it, and what finally convinced you?
questions: Mary arrives in the dark and assumes the worst: "They have taken the Lord out of the tomb" (v. 2). Why do you think grief makes it hard to see what is actually in front of us?
Jesus asks Mary, "Woman, why are you weeping?" (v. 15). If Jesus asked you that question today, what would you tell him?
Mary does not recognize Jesus until he says her name: "Mary" (v. 16). What does it mean to you that he knows people by name?

The disciples are meeting "with the doors locked for fear of the Jews" (v. 19), and Jesus says, "Peace be with you!" What are you afraid of right now, and what would it look like to hear that greeting there?
Jesus says, "As the Father has sent Me, so also I am sending you" (v. 21). Where do you sense you are being sent: home, work, school, your neighborhood?

Thomas says he will not believe unless he sees the nail marks (v. 25). Jesus does not scold him but offers what he asked for. What does that tell you about how Jesus treats honest doubt, and how might it shape the way we treat each other?
Jesus says, "blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed" (v. 29). What helps your faith when you cannot see or feel much? What makes it harder?
20.life: This week, when worry or doubt comes up, say Thomas's words quietly to Jesus: "My Lord and my God!" (v. 28). If you have an honest question, tell him that too, and share it with one trusted person in the group.
20.prayer: Thank Jesus that he comes to frightened and doubting people and says, "Peace be with you." Ask for peace for anyone in the group who is afraid, grieving or unsure.
20.tip: Thomas is often reduced to a label. Do not let the group use his story to shame doubters or to push anyone to say they are certain. Point out that Jesus meets Thomas where he is. Also, two spots are puzzling: Jesus' words to Mary in verse 17 and the forgiveness words in verse 23. Christians read them differently, so say that plainly and move on.

21.open: Have you ever gone back to something familiar, like an old job, an old hobby or your hometown, when you weren't sure what came next?
questions: Peter says, "I am going fishing," and the others go with him (v. 3). Why do you think they went back to the boats, and when have you gone back to something familiar while waiting for clarity?
They worked all night and "caught nothing" (v. 3). Then one word from the shore changes everything. Where do you feel like you have been working hard with little to show for it?
Jesus has a fire going and says, "Come, have breakfast" (v. 12). What does it tell you about Jesus that his first move is to feed tired friends?

Jesus asks Peter, "do you love Me?" three times (vv. 15-17). Peter had denied Jesus three times, and the setting is another charcoal fire. What do you think Jesus is doing here, and why might it matter that it happens out loud?

Peter answers, "Lord, You know all things," and then says that Jesus knows he loves him (v. 17). What would it be like to say that to Jesus honestly, with your own failures in mind? If you are unsure how you would answer, what makes it hard?
Each time Peter answers, Jesus gives him work to do: "Feed My lambs," "Shepherd My sheep" (vv. 15-16). Why might being trusted with something be part of a real fresh start?
Peter asks about the other disciple, and Jesus answers, "what is that to you? You follow Me!" (v. 22). When are you most tempted to compare your path with someone else's?

Christians read Jesus' words to Peter differently. Some see a special leadership role for Peter and those after him, and others see mainly a personal restoration. What stands out to you in the way Jesus treats Peter, whichever way you read it?
21.life: Think of one person you have let down, or one failure you keep replaying. This week, take one small step: say sorry, accept a forgiveness you have been holding at arm's length, or tell Jesus in your own words that you love him, even if it feels shaky. Then do one simple thing to care for someone else.
21.prayer: Thank Jesus for meeting us with breakfast and not blame. Ask him to heal the places where we feel disqualified, and for help to follow him without comparing ourselves to others.
21.tip: Question 5 and the failure theme can touch real shame, so do not push anyone to share. Let people answer in general terms, and make clear that Jesus asks Peter the question gently, never as a trap. Verse 17 says Peter was "deeply hurt," so it is fine for the group to admit that honest conversations with God can sting.
